claims.text: The initial alloy has a dual-phase microstructure consisting of a disordered FCC matrix and an ordered B2 phase.
The initial FCC/B2 alloy is metastable, has fine phase boundaries, and has minimal long-range ordering within the FCC matrix.
Aging at approximately 600–800 °C evolves LCO and coarsens B2 domains without causing grain coarsening or impurity segregation.
Intermediate aging is below the thresholds for full phase decomposition and recrystallization but above the threshold for rapid LCO nucleation.
Percolation of ordered B2 domains through LCO evolution drives the transient ductile-brittle-ductile transition.
Percolating LCO and B2 domains create a critical threshold of dislocation pinning at phase boundaries.
Critical LCO size and connectivity force dislocations to cross-slip or break down into super-dislocations.
Ordered regions force dislocations to bow around or cut through them, producing super-dislocations and localized phase-boundary stress concentrations.
During aging, LCO develops from short-range to medium-range order.
Increasing LCO locally raises stacking-fault energy and promotes ordered B2 precipitation.
Percolating ordered domains restrict dislocation cross-slip and cause a transition from planar slip to localized shear banding or brittle fracture.
At higher aging temperatures, thermal energy overcomes ordering enthalpy, dissolves LCO clusters or reduces their coherence, and thereby restores cross-slip and ductility.
Initial aging increases strength while retaining ductility.
A critical aging time or temperature produces a sharp ductility loss when LCO domains percolate.
Further aging restores ductility as LCO dissolves or transforms.
The embrittlement regime occurs when the LCO correlation length exceeds a critical dislocation spacing of approximately 10–50 nm and ends before B2 disordering or significant FCC grain growth.
Higher cooling rates, altered alloying, or an ordering-inhibiting solute can suppress LCO formation.
A control with suppressed LCO should show monotonic softening or no brittle transition.
Concurrent measurements of LCO size and connectivity, phase-boundary morphology, dislocation structure, and tensile ductility can discriminate the LCO/PB mechanism from a grain-boundary mechanism.
The hypothesis is falsified by a ductility drop without increased LCO size or connectivity, persistent ductility despite percolating LCO, or the same brittle transition in an LCO-suppressed control.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says critical ordering forces dislocations to cross-slip, whereas the mechanism says percolating ordered domains restrict cross-slip and that restored cross-slip produces ductility.

Recovery is attributed to higher aging temperature in the mechanism but to further aging in the predicted outcome, conflating temperature-driven disordering with time-dependent evolution at a fixed temperature.
